pos: n. (proper name; an ancestor of Christ in Luke's genealogy)
etymology: Greek Melea, of uncertain derivation, perhaps from a Hebrew root signifying fulness; named once, in the line of Nathan the son of David.
biblical_def: Melea is one of the men in the stretch of Luke's genealogy that runs from David to the exile through Nathan rather than through Solomon. He is named once: “Which was the son of Melea, which was the son of Menan, which was the son of Mattatha, which was the son of Nathan, which was the son of David” (Luke 3:31). The verse that follows carries the line back past David into the house of Jesse and Boaz: “Which was the son of Jesse, which was the son of Obed, which was the son of Booz, which was the son of Salmon, which was the son of Naasson” (Luke 3:32). Nothing else of Melea is on record — no deed, no city, no wife, no word. He is a link, and the chain is the point. Isaiah had promised a rod out of a cut stem: “And there shall come forth a rod out of the stem of Jesse, and a Branch shall grow out of his roots” (Isaiah 11:1), and Paul says flatly that the promise was kept in the flesh: “Concerning his Son Jesus Christ our Lord, which was made of the seed of David according to the flesh” (Romans 1:3). Between the promise and the fulfilment lie a thousand years and a long row of unremarkable men, of whom Melea is one, each of whom had to live and beget a son for the Branch to come.

corruption_paragraphs: Readers skip the lists, and preachers skip them too, on the ground that nothing happens in them. A great deal happens in them. Every name is a generation in which the promise to David might have failed and did not. Melea did nothing the record keeps except live and father a son, and the Branch out of Jesse came by way of him.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God keeps covenant across centuries through unremarkable lives, and that a man whose name is all that survives of him may yet have been essential to the coming of Christ.

pos: n. (proper name; an ancestor of Christ in Luke's genealogy)
etymology: Greek Mainan, of uncertain derivation; named once, in the line from David through Nathan.
biblical_def: Menan is named once in Scripture, in the Nathan branch of Luke's genealogy of Christ: “Which was the son of Melea, which was the son of Menan, which was the son of Mattatha, which was the son of Nathan, which was the son of David” (Luke 3:31). He stands four generations below David. The oath that makes his existence significant was sworn long before he was born: “And when thy days be fulfilled, and thou shalt sleep with thy fathers, I will set up thy seed after thee, which shall proceed out of thy bowels, and I will establish his kingdom” (2 Samuel 7:12). Peter, preaching at Pentecost, treats that oath as the hinge of the resurrection: “Therefore being a prophet, and knowing that God had sworn with an oath to him, that of the fruit of his loins, according to the flesh, he would raise up Christ to sit on his throne” (Acts 2:30). Luke's list in that place also names Simeon, Juda, Joseph, Jonan and Eliakim: “Which was the son of Simeon, which was the son of Juda, which was the son of Joseph, which was the son of Jonan, which was the son of Eliakim” (Luke 3:30). Menan belongs to that company of men whose only recorded act is to have stood where God had promised a line would stand.

pos: n. (proper name; a grandson of David through Nathan, and an ancestor of Christ)
etymology: Greek Mattatha, from Hebrew Mattattah, gift of the LORD, from mattan, a gift, and a shortened form of the divine name.
biblical_def: Mattatha is the grandson of David named in Luke's genealogy, the son of Nathan: “Which was the son of Melea, which was the son of Menan, which was the son of Mattatha, which was the son of Nathan, which was the son of David” (Luke 3:31). The Nathan here is David's son, born in Jerusalem and listed with Solomon among the children of the king: “And these be the names of those that were born unto him in Jerusalem; Shammua, and Shobab, and Nathan, and Solomon” (2 Samuel 5:14). That Luke's line runs through Nathan rather than Solomon is no small matter; Zechariah had marked the house of Nathan as a distinct family in the royal mourning: “And the land shall mourn, every family apart; the family of the house of David apart, and their wives apart; the family of the house of Nathan apart, and their wives apart” (Zechariah 12:12). From Mattatha the list goes on through Menan and Melea toward Jesse's older stock: “Which was the son of Jesse, which was the son of Obed, which was the son of Booz, which was the son of Salmon, which was the son of Naasson” (Luke 3:32). His name means gift of the LORD, which is the fittest title a man in such a list could bear.

pos: n. (proper name; an ancestor of Christ in Luke's genealogy)
etymology: Greek Ioreim, probably a shortened Greek form of a Hebrew name compounded with Yah, the LORD; named once, at Luke 3:29.
biblical_def: Jorim is named once in all of Scripture, in the post-exilic stretch of Luke's genealogy: “Which was the son of Jose, which was the son of Eliezer, which was the son of Jorim, which was the son of Matthat, which was the son of Levi” (Luke 3:29). The names around him are equally silent in the rest of the Bible: “Which was the son of Melchi, which was the son of Addi, which was the son of Cosam, which was the son of Elmodam, which was the son of Er” (Luke 3:28), and “Which was the son of Simeon, which was the son of Juda, which was the son of Joseph, which was the son of Jonan, which was the son of Eliakim” (Luke 3:30). These are the four centuries between the last prophet and the angel in the temple, when there was no voice from God in Israel and the line of promise simply went on living in villages. Then the silence broke: “But when the fulness of the time was come, God sent forth his Son, made of a woman, made under the law” (Galatians 4:4). The fulness of the time was not an empty interval that God filled at last; it was a measured span, and men like Jorim were the measure of it.

pos: n. (proper name; an ancestor of Christ in Luke's genealogy)
etymology: Greek Iose, a shortened form of Joseph or of Jose's Hebrew original; named once, at Luke 3:29. He is a distinct man from Joses of the New Testament, the brother of our Lord and the surname of Barnabas.
biblical_def: Jose is named once, in Luke's genealogy of our Lord: “Which was the son of Jose, which was the son of Eliezer, which was the son of Jorim, which was the son of Matthat, which was the son of Levi” (Luke 3:29). The names on either side of him are from the same obscure stretch: “Which was the son of Melchi, which was the son of Addi, which was the son of Cosam, which was the son of Elmodam, which was the son of Er” (Luke 3:28), and “Which was the son of Simeon, which was the son of Juda, which was the son of Joseph, which was the son of Jonan, which was the son of Eliakim” (Luke 3:30). Twice in this part of the list the name Levi appears, and it is worth noticing what the writer to the Hebrews says about the tribe from which our Lord actually sprang: “For it is evident that our Lord sprang out of Juda; of which tribe Moses spake nothing concerning priesthood” (Hebrews 7:14). Men in Christ's line bore Levitical names without being Levites, and the Lord who came of Judah holds a priesthood the law of Moses never provided for. That is the argument of Hebrews, and it rests on a genealogy.

pos: n. (proper name; an ancestor of Christ in Luke's genealogy)
etymology: Greek Naggai, from Hebrew Nogah, brightness or shining; named once, at Luke 3:25.
biblical_def: Nagge is named once, among the generations of Luke's genealogy that lie between the exile and the birth of Christ: “Which was the son of Mattathias, which was the son of Amos, which was the son of Naum, which was the son of Esli, which was the son of Nagge” (Luke 3:25). The verses on either side are of the same character: “Which was the son of Matthat, which was the son of Levi, which was the son of Melchi, which was the son of Janna, which was the son of Joseph” (Luke 3:24), and “Which was the son of Maath, which was the son of Mattathias, which was the son of Semei, which was the son of Joseph, which was the son of Juda” (Luke 3:26). His name comes from a Hebrew word for brightness, and the promise his family carried was of a throne: “He shall be great, and shall be called the Son of the Highest: and the Lord God shall give unto him the throne of his father David” (Luke 1:32). That angelic word was spoken to Mary a few generations after Nagge, and it took up a hope his whole line had been keeping while the house of David held no throne at all. Men named for brightness lived in the dark and died in it, and the light came.

pos: n. (proper name; an ancestor of Christ in Luke's genealogy)
etymology: Greek Ianna, probably a shortened form of a Hebrew name compounded with the divine name, as Johanan; named once, at Luke 3:24.
biblical_def: Janna stands three generations above Joseph the husband of Mary in Luke's genealogy: “Which was the son of Matthat, which was the son of Levi, which was the son of Melchi, which was the son of Janna, which was the son of Joseph” (Luke 3:24). The list begins with a careful parenthesis about the legal fatherhood of Christ: “And Jesus himself began to be about thirty years of age, being (as was supposed) the son of Joseph, which was the son of Heli” (Luke 3:23). The words as was supposed are the evangelist's guard on the virgin birth: Joseph was reckoned the father and was not. The line runs on through names recorded nowhere else: “Which was the son of Mattathias, which was the son of Amos, which was the son of Naum, which was the son of Esli, which was the son of Nagge” (Luke 3:25), and it ends, far down the chapter, at the head of the whole race: “Which was the son of Enos, which was the son of Seth, which was the son of Adam, which was the son of God” (Luke 3:38). Janna is one unknown link in a chain that Luke runs from Christ all the way back to Adam, because the Saviour he preaches is the Saviour of men as men.

pos: n. (proper name; the father of Salathiel in Luke's genealogy, and an ancestor of Christ)
etymology: Greek Neri, from Hebrew Neriyah, the LORD is my lamp, from ner, a lamp, with the divine name.
biblical_def: Neri is named once, and his place in the list is one of the most discussed in the New Testament: “Which was the son of Joanna, which was the son of Rhesa, which was the son of Zorobabel, which was the son of Salathiel, which was the son of Neri” (Luke 3:27). Matthew gives Salathiel a different father, Jechonias of the Solomonic kings; Luke gives him Neri, of the house of Nathan. The ordinary and sufficient explanation is that Jechonias' line failed of natural heirs and the inheritance passed to the nearest kinsman out of Nathan's branch, so that Salathiel was Neri's son by birth and Jechonias' by law. The names around Neri are from the same quiet stretch: “Which was the son of Maath, which was the son of Mattathias, which was the son of Semei, which was the son of Joseph, which was the son of Juda” (Luke 3:26), and “Which was the son of Melchi, which was the son of Addi, which was the son of Cosam, which was the son of Elmodam, which was the son of Er” (Luke 3:28). Jeremiah's promise stands over the whole problem: “Behold, the days come, saith the LORD, that I will raise unto David a righteous Branch, and a King shall reign and prosper, and shall execute judgment and justice in the earth” (Jeremiah 23:5). The LORD is my lamp, says Neri's name, and the lamp of David did not go out.

corruption_paragraphs: That Matthew and Luke give Salathiel two different fathers is offered as proof that the gospels contradict. The law of Israel accounts for it without strain: where a line failed, the inheritance and the legal sonship passed to the nearest kinsman. Luke records the blood, Matthew the title. Both lists end in Christ, and the crown and the body both reached Him.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God preserved a righteous Branch for David through a judgment that cut off the reigning house, and that the lamp He promised was not extinguished by the exile.

pos: n. (proper name; an ancestor of Christ in Luke's genealogy)
etymology: Greek Maath, of uncertain derivation, perhaps from a Hebrew root signifying small or few; named once, at Luke 3:26.
biblical_def: Maath is named once in Scripture: “Which was the son of Maath, which was the son of Mattathias, which was the son of Semei, which was the son of Joseph, which was the son of Juda” (Luke 3:26). The generations on either hand are as little known: “Which was the son of Mattathias, which was the son of Amos, which was the son of Naum, which was the son of Esli, which was the son of Nagge” (Luke 3:25), and “Which was the son of Joanna, which was the son of Rhesa, which was the son of Zorobabel, which was the son of Salathiel, which was the son of Neri” (Luke 3:27). Matthew opens his gospel with the royal and covenantal summary of the same descent: “The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, the son of David, the son of Abraham” (Matthew 1:1). Two names carry Matthew's whole heading, David and Abraham, because those are the two to whom the promises were made. Maath is one of the men between the promise and the keeping of it. His name may well mean small, and that is the honest size of him in the record — a small man in a great line, which is the position of nearly everyone God uses.

corruption_summary: Significance is measured by scale; Maath is a small man in the line of the son of David, the son of Abraham.
corruption_paragraphs: Men want to matter visibly, and a name in a list seems the opposite of mattering. But the whole of Matthew's heading rests on two promises, to David and to Abraham, and the keeping of those promises ran through hundreds of men of whom Scripture records nothing but that they were born and begat. That is not insignificance; it is service of a kind that leaves no monument.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the promises to Abraham and David are the frame of the gospel, and that God carries them by means of the small.

etymology: Greek Ionan, probably from Hebrew Yohanan, the LORD is gracious, or from Yonah, a dove; named once, at Luke 3:30.
biblical_def: Jonan is named once in Scripture: “Which was the son of Simeon, which was the son of Juda, which was the son of Joseph, which was the son of Jonan, which was the son of Eliakim” (Luke 3:30). He stands in the long middle of Luke's list, between the names of the post-exilic generations: “Which was the son of Jose, which was the son of Eliezer, which was the son of Jorim, which was the son of Matthat, which was the son of Levi” (Luke 3:29) before him, and the branch of David's son Nathan after: “Which was the son of Melea, which was the son of Menan, which was the son of Mattatha, which was the son of Nathan, which was the son of David” (Luke 3:31). And Luke carries the whole line past Abraham, past Noah, to the beginning: “Which was the son of Enos, which was the son of Seth, which was the son of Adam, which was the son of God” (Luke 3:38). That last clause is the reason the genealogy exists where it does in the gospel. Luke places it immediately after the baptism, where the Father says Thou art my beloved Son, and then traces the man standing in Jordan back to Adam, who was the son of God by creation. The second Adam is set against the first.

corruption_summary: Christ is treated as the founder of one religion among many; Luke traces Him to Adam, making Him the second head of the whole race.
corruption_paragraphs: If our Lord were merely the head of a nation or a sect, a Jewish genealogy to Abraham would suffice, and Matthew gives one. Luke runs the line past Abraham to Adam, the son of God by creation, and sets the Man baptized in Jordan over against the man who fell in the garden. The claim is not tribal. It is upon every son of Adam alive.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that Christ is the last Adam and the second man, the federal head of a new humanity, and that this is taught by the shape of Luke's genealogy itself.
